refs.supports: Supports the claim that a UBI would shift transfers toward childless, nonelderly, nondisabled and middle-income households compared with existing US programs. It also supports the claim that a UBI generous enough to raise transfers to low-income families would be 'enormously expensive'. That fiscal barrier is the one the enactment-hazard priors must price in advanced countries. The review also covers labor-supply evidence and argues that pilots will do little to settle the main open questions.

The developing-country counterpart to Hoynes and Rothstein. It reviews what is known and unknown about three questions: how recipients use extra income, whether a UBI would unlock growth, and whether universal payments beat targeted ones. Cite it for the argument that the economics and politics of a UBI differ between countries with and without mature safety nets. It does not give enactment probabilities.

refs.supports: Defines political feasibility in probabilistic terms: a 'reasonable probability of the policy becoming actualized in the foreseeable future'. That definition motivates treating enactment as a forecastable probability. It crosses agency (discrete vs. diffuse) with constraints (prospective vs. retrospective) to get four types: strategic, institutional, psychological and behavioral feasibility. The paper can map its government-control and enactment-hazard terms onto the prospective cells. That mapping is the paper's own, not the authors'.

refs.supports: Uses the ESS round 8 (2016) question in 23 countries, which describes a BI as universal, unconditional, tax-financed and replacing other benefits. Support is 'relatively high, but varying' across countries and groups. It is higher among economically vulnerable, left-leaning, egalitarian and younger respondents, and in countries with more material deprivation. It is evidence on stated support, not on enactment. Caveat: the article labels code LT as 'Latvia' (its top-support country), but LT is Lithuania in ESS 8. Cite the country as Lithuania or not at all.

refs.supports: Uses ESS 2016 multilevel models to show that a broader coalition of UBI supporters appears where social spending is low. Welfare chauvinism and ideology matter more for UBI attitudes in high-spending countries. The authors call this a 'demand-capacity paradox': countries least equipped to implement a UBI show the broadest support. It supports treating high stated support as weak evidence of enactment capacity when setting cross-country priors.

A research note using ESS data for 21 countries. It finds no association between an individual's job-automation risk and UBI support, and finds demand for UBI lower than demand for redistribution. This is a caution for the AI-labor-shock channel: pre-shock automation exposure has not translated into UBI support, so the shock-to-enactment link must work through something other than existing risk-driven preferences. Busemeyer and Sahm (2022, Journal of Social Policy 51(4):751-770, doi:10.1017/S0047279421000519, also verified) likewise find no significant automation-risk association with basic-income support.

The historical near-miss case: guaranteed-income plans had broad bipartisan support in the 1960s, and Nixon's Family Assistance Plan 'nearly passed into law'. Carter later advanced a similar bill. Steensland attributes the failure partly to stakeholders and institutions, and centrally to culture: the plans challenged the distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor. This supports keeping enactment hazards well below 1 even when the governing coalition favors the policy.

Finnish support is 60-70% in principle but falls to about 30% when respondents are told taxes would rise. Advocates are a diffuse group without discrete power, and there are institutional and EU-level constraints. It concludes that 'for the time being universal basic income is not a realistic policy option' in Finland. That directly informs a low Finnish enactment prior and shows how cost framing moves stated support.

refs.supports: The peer-reviewed employment estimate from Finland's experiment. It randomized 2,000 unemployment-benefit recipients to a basic income, which cut participation tax rates for full-time work by 23 percentage points. Days in employment were statistically unchanged in the first year. Use it for the finding that the only nationwide randomized BI trial produced minor employment effects at best. It is not evidence about a full-population UBI.

The OpenResearch RCT randomized 1,000 low-income people to $1,000 a month for three years, against 2,000 controls receiving $50 a month. Non-transfer income fell about $1,900 a year, and labor-market participation fell 4.2 percentage points. Hours fell 1-2 a week, with a similar reduction for partners. The authors call it a moderate labor-supply effect. It is still a working paper (July 2024, revised August 2026, no journal version listed). Cite the revision's numbers; earlier versions reported different magnitudes.

Every Alaska resident has received a yearly dividend since 1982. Using CPS data and synthetic control, the authors find no effect on employment and a 1.8 percentage point (17 percent) rise in part-time work, consistent with local general-equilibrium stimulus. Cite it as evidence that a universal, permanent, unconditional transfer exists subnationally and did not significantly reduce aggregate employment. Not verified: whether the dividend clears the paper's share-of-GDP-per-head threshold.

Iran's 2011 program paid monthly cash into individual accounts for more than 70 million people, worth 28% of median per capita household income. It compensated for the removal of energy subsidies. Panel evidence shows no reduction in hours or participation, and positive effects for women and self-employed men. Cite it as the closest national-scale precedent, enacted as subsidy compensation. The 28% is relative to median per capita household income, not GDP per head, so don't apply it directly to the paper's threshold.

refs.supports: Task-based framework in which automation displaces labor while new tasks reinstate it; over three decades of US industry data, slower employment growth reflects faster automation, weaker new-task creation, and slower productivity growth. Use it to justify modeling the AI labor shock as net displacement that depends on whether reinstatement keeps pace, not as automatic job loss.

Historical counterweight: past automation did not eliminate most jobs because it complemented labor, raised output demand, and created new work, though recent decades show polarization. Use it to justify putting substantial prior mass on no transformative labor shock within the forecast horizon.

Policy Forum estimating US task exposure to LLMs: about 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks exposed to LLMs with simple interfaces, rising to just over 46% once complementary software is counted. Use it as evidence that exposure is broad but that realized effects depend on complementary tooling and diffusion, which supports a lagged, uncertain shock-timing prior. Exposure is not displacement.

The AEA landing page citation meta gives Acemoglu and Restrepo, JEP 33(2): 3-30, 2019/05, DOI 10.1257/jep.33.2.3, and Crossref matches. A decomposition of US industry data attributes the slower growth of labor demand in 1987-2017, relative to 1947-1987, to accelerated displacement, weaker reinstatement (new-task creation) and slower productivity growth. Use it to justify modeling the AI labor shock as net displacement that depends on whether reinstatement keeps pace, not as automatic job loss.

The PDF footer reads 'Vol. 84, Article 9. Publication date: October 2025', 48 pages, DOI 10.1613/jair.1.19087, which resolves. arXiv 2401.02843 carries the same title and journal DOI. The abstract confirms 2,778 respondents surveyed in October 2023, HLMI at 10% by 2027 and 50% by 2047, and FAOL at 10% by 2037 and 50% by 2116. The overstatement: both questions tell respondents 'Think feasibility, not adoption', and FAOL means all occupations becoming 'fully automatable'. It does not mean they are actually automated. The supports sentence's 'full automation of all occupations' and 'outperforming humans at every task' read as realized automation, which matters when the forecast is used to time a labor shock. The paper also conditions on science continuing undisrupted. The BibTeX is correct as given.
checks.supports_fix: October 2023 survey of 2,778 researchers who had published at top AI venues. Assuming science continues undisrupted, the aggregate forecast gives a 10% chance by 2027 and 50% by 2047 that unaided machines could accomplish every task better and more cheaply than humans. It gives 10% by 2037 and 50% by 2116 that all occupations become fully automatable. Respondents were told to think of feasibility, not adoption. Use it as one expert anchor for the wide dispersion in AI capability timing, which needs a further adoption lag before any labor shock. Note that answers differ sharply with question framing and reflect researcher opinion, not calibrated forecasts.

checks.evidence: NBER page meta: Anton Korinek and Donghyun Suh, 'Scenarios for the Transition to AGI', Working Paper 32255, issue date March 2024 (2024/03/18), DOI 10.3386/w32255, which resolves to the NBER PDF. No journal version was found (it is also arXiv 2403.12107). The abstract says the effect on wages 'depend[s] on a race between automation and capital accumulation'. If automation is sufficiently slow, 'wages may rise forever'. If task complexity is bounded and full automation is reached, 'wages collapse'. Declines may come even before that if automation outpaces capital accumulation. The supports sentence is faithful. 'Slow automation lets wages rise indefinitely' slightly strengthens 'sufficiently slow ... may rise forever', which is acceptable.

The OUP landing page (via WebFetch) and Crossref give Acemoglu, 'The simple macroeconomics of AI', Economic Policy 40(121): 13-58, January 2025 issue (online 6 August 2024), DOI 10.1093/epolic/eiae042, which resolves to academic.oup.com. The abstract (NBER w32487 and OUP) invokes 'a version of Hulten's theorem'. It gives 'no more than a 0.66% increase' in TFP over 10 years, and less than 0.53% once hard-to-learn tasks are accounted for. AI is 'unlikely to increase inequality as much as previous automation' but will 'widen the gap between capital and labor income'. The abstract also says there is no evidence AI will reduce labor-income inequality. The supports sentence is accurate. The TFP figures are for the US economy.

refs.supports: The chapter abstract, read on the Springer landing page, defines decomposition. You split an estimation task into components that are easier to estimate, then combine them into the target estimate. It says decomposition is used most for highly uncertain estimates. It warns that multiplicative decomposition is 'especially sensitive to correlated errors in component values' and should be used only when the components can be estimated more accurately than the target. That supports the paper's split into timing × control × hazard, and it names the main risk: correlated errors across the parts. The reference lists of other chapters cite the book as Kluwer Academic Publishers (Norwell, MA). Springer and Crossref now list it as Springer, Boston, MA. Pages 107–123 come from Crossref.

This is the original PERT paper, written for the Polaris Fleet Ballistic Missile program. Its abstract on the INFORMS page says technical experts elicit elapsed-time estimates for activities, which are 'subsequently expressed in probability terms'. Cite it as the origin of PERT-style elicitation from experts. I could not open the full text: the INFORMS PDF is paywalled and there is no open-access copy. So I did not confirm that the three-point (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) beta formulas appear in it. Say 'PERT-style priors' rather than attributing a specific formula to this paper. If the paper uses a specific beta-PERT parameterization, cite its source separately. Page range 646–669 comes from Crossref and EconPapers; the INFORMS page shows only the issue range.

An optional companion to Malcolm et al. Clark was a coauthor of the 1959 paper. The abstract on the INFORMS page says this note answers 'whence the statements in that paper concerning the distribution of an activity time'. Cite it for where the PERT activity-time distribution comes from. The letter's text could not be extracted: the PDF has no text layer, so only its abstract was read. Don't cite it for a specific formula until someone reads the two pages.

The standard survey. Its abstract (AEA and NBER pages) says market forecasts are typically fairly accurate, beat most moderately sophisticated benchmarks, and that suitable contracts reveal market probabilities. For caveats on thin markets, I read the text of NBER WP w10504 (May 2004), not the JEP PDF, which returned 403. It says markets are 'likely' to do poorly on small-probability events (favorite–longshot bias), more so on smaller exchanges. It says manipulability depends partly on how thin a market is, and that markets fail without a motivation to trade. It also reports that very thin internal markets (20–60 traders) did strikingly well. Cite both sides when comparing the model with thin Manifold markets.

The paper compared play-money NewsFutures with real-money TradeSports over 208 NFL games (4 Sep–8 Dec 2003). The play-money market 'performed as well as' the real-money one. Both beat most of the 1,947 individual contestants in a ProbabilityFootball contest. Cite it for the claim that a play-money market need not be less accurate than a real-money one. The setting was liquid and short-horizon, though: about 100 traders per game on NewsFutures, with outcomes resolving within days. So it does not show that thin, decades-out markets are reliable. I checked the T&F landing page and the authors' PDF (volume, issue and pages are printed on it).

The paper documents the favorite–long shot bias in horse-race betting: long shots are overbet and favorites are underbet. Using win bets plus exacta, quinella and trifecta bets, it finds evidence that misperceptions of probability drive the bias, not risk-love. Cite it for why low-probability prices may be too high. The evidence is from pari-mutuel horse racing. Applying it to low-probability UBI markets on Manifold is the paper's own inference and should be worded that way. I checked the JPE landing page, which gives Vol 118 No 4, August 2010, pp. 723–746; the NBER w15923 page agrees.

A textbook source for the maths behind the signposts. Chapter 2, 'Conditional probability' (pp. 45–101), covers the law of total probability. Chapter 9, 'Conditional expectation' (pp. 415–456), extends it to expectations; the chapter abstract makes that link. Applied to the indicator of enactment, this gives E[P(H|E)] = P(H). So the conditional forecasts in the signposts, weighted by the probability of each signpost, must average back to the headline forecast. I verified the chapter titles and page ranges through Crossref and the T&F page, not theorem numbers, so cite by chapter. I did not verify whether the book uses the name 'conservation of expected evidence'; see yudkowsky2007conservation for the name.

Optional. This is where the name comes from. The post states that the expected posterior must equal the prior, and gives P(H) = P(H|E)P(E) + P(H|¬E)P(¬E). Cite it only as credit for the name alongside the textbook, not as the mathematical source. Sources disagree on the day (12 or 13 Aug 2007, likely a time-zone difference), so the entry gives only the month.

On 21 Sep 2026, Metaculus announced Radiant in open beta, with free credits during the beta. It is a visual map of the predictions behind a decision. Each box holds a live Metaculus forecast, a base rate or a team estimate, with its source attached. A range in a box 'carries the whole range forward instead of rounding it to a single number' in any formula that reads it. An AI assistant drafts first maps. Cite it as a current tool that decomposes decisions and propagates uncertainty, like the paper's approach. The post does not say how ranges are propagated (Monte Carlo or otherwise), so don't claim a mechanism. The post also calls Metaculus 'a forecasting platform (not a prediction market)', which helps if the paper contrasts it with Manifold. The byline is 'Metaculus'; the date comes from the page's datetime field.

Crossref gives the book subtitle 'A Handbook for Researchers and Practitioners', publisher Springer US, Boston, MA, and pages 107-123. The abstract, read verbatim, says 'multiplicative decomposition is especially sensitive to correlated errors in component values'. It says decomposition is 'most used for highly uncertain estimates'. It says to use it only when components can be estimated 'more accurately or more confidently than the target estimate'.
checks.supports_fix: Minor: the abstract's condition is 'more accurately or more confidently', not just 'more accurately'. The chapter is about judgmental point estimation, so the paper should present it as a general rationale for the timing x control x hazard split. It does not validate Monte Carlo propagation specifically.

checks.evidence: doi.org/10.1287/opre.7.5.646 resolves to INFORMS. The page is Cloudflare-blocked (403) for me, so I read the abstract from its Crossref deposit instead. Crossref gives D. G. Malcolm, J. H. Roseboom, C. E. Clark, W. Fazar, Operations Research 7(5):646-669, issued 1959-10; RePEc/IDEAS agrees. The abstract describes the Polaris FBM program. It says 'The time estimates are obtained from responsible technical persons and are subsequently expressed in probability terms.' I could not access the full text. Secondary sources (a web-search summary and a rare-book dealer) credit the paper with three-point beta estimates, but I did not verify that in the primary text, so the hedge is right.
checks.supports_fix: Fix the paraphrase. The abstract says the estimates are obtained FROM responsible technical persons; it does not say 'technical experts elicit' them. Keep 'PERT-style priors' and do not attribute the (a+4m+b)/6 formulas to this paper unless someone reads the full text.

checks.evidence: doi.org/10.1287/opre.10.3.405 resolves to INFORMS, which is Cloudflare-blocked (403) for me. Crossref and RePEc/IDEAS both give Charles E. The AEA landing page gives Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz, 'Prediction Markets', JEP 18(2):107-126, Spring 2004, DOI 10.1257/0895330041371321, which resolves. The abstract says market forecasts 'are typically fairly accurate' and 'outperform most moderately sophisticated benchmarks'. I read the full text of NBER w10504 (May 2004). It says 'it is likely that prediction markets will also perform poorly at predicting small probability events'. It says TradeSports mispricing is 'consistent with the longshot bias being more pronounced on smaller-scale exchanges'. It says manipulability depends 'at least in part' on how thin markets are, and that 'Even well-designed markets will fail unless a motivation to trade exists.' It says the HP and Siemens markets (20-60 people) were 'very thin markets' whose performance 'was quite striking'. All of this matches the supports text.
checks.supports_fix: Optional: say that the caveats are quoted from the NBER working-paper version, and that the JEP text may be worded slightly differently.

checks.evidence: The DOI resolves (T&F/Informa); the T&F landing page is Cloudflare-blocked for me. Crossref gives Servan-Schreiber, Wolfers, Pennock and Galebach, Electronic Markets 14(3):243-251, Sept 2004. The authors' PDF (users.nber.org/~jwolfers/Papers/DoesMoneyMatter.pdf) prints 'Volume 14 (3): 243-251' and the DOI. The text gives 208 NFL games from 4 Sep to 8 Dec 2003. It says NewsFutures averaged about 100 traders per game (rarely under 50 or over 200). There were 1,947 ProbabilityFootball participants at week 14. Both markets ranked in the top 1% (11th and 12th), and finished 6th and 8th by season's end. The abstract says the play-money markets 'performed as well as the real-money markets'. The supports text is accurate, and so is its caveat about liquid, short-horizon markets.

doi.org/10.1086/655844 resolves to journals.uchicago.edu, which is Cloudflare-blocked for me. Crossref gives Erik Snowberg and Justin Wolfers, 'Explaining the Favorite-Long Shot Bias: Is it Risk-Love or Misperceptions?', JPE 118(4):723-746, August 2010. The NBER w15923 page gives the same published citation. Its abstract says 'longshots are overbet, while favorites are underbet'. It tests using win bets plus exacta, quinella and trifecta pools, and finds 'misperceptions of probability drive the favorite-longshot bias'. The supports text is accurate, and it rightly says that applying this to Manifold is the paper's own inference.

doi.org/10.1201/9780429428357 resolves to taylorfrancis.com. Crossref gives Joseph K. Blitzstein and Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability, edition 2, Chapman and Hall/CRC, published 2019-02-08. The T&F page title is 'Introduction to Probability, Second Edition' (print ISBN 9781138369917 appears in the jacket image URL). Chapter DOIs from Crossref: -2 'Conditional probability' is pp. 45-101; -9 'Conditional expectation' is pp. 415-456. Both resolve. The chapter 9 abstract on T&F says the law of total probability gets unconditional probabilities by slicing the sample space, and that 'The same idea works for computing unconditional expectations.' The supports text is accurate, and its hedges (cite by chapter; the book may not use the name) are right.

The LessWrong page shows 'Conservation of Expected Evidence' by Eliezer Yudkowsky, 13th Aug 2007, cross-posted from Overcoming Bias. The LessWrong GraphQL API gives postedAt 2007-08-13T15:55:26Z. The post says 'the expectation of the posterior probability, after viewing the evidence, must equal the prior probability'. It gives P(H) = P(H|E)P(E) + P(H|~E)P(~E). A month-only BibTeX entry is valid.
checks.supports_fix: The note about the date is shaky. LessWrong's timestamp is 15:55 UTC on 13 Aug 2007, which falls on 13 Aug in every US time zone, so a time-zone difference does not explain a 12 Aug date. I did not check the original Overcoming Bias page (Wayback returned 429). Either give day = 13 from LessWrong, or keep month only without the time-zone explanation.
